summary: Analyzes security threats against the Access Node Control Protocol (ANCP), which carries QoS and subscriber configuration between a network access server and an access node such as a DSLAM. It then lists the security requirements the protocol should meet. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC works out who could attack the protocol a provider uses to tell its street cabinet what quality of service to give each line, what they could do, and what the protocol must therefore provide. It covers denial of service, tampering with messages, forcing weaker protection, and misconfiguring the cabinet.

subtitle: Who could attack the protocol between a provider's server and its street cabinet, and what it must do about them.

tldr.problem: The Access Node Control Protocol carries quality-of-service and subscriber configuration between a network access server and the access node at the end of the line, and nothing in the network stops an attacker from interfering with it.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC builds a threat model of the system, lists five kinds of attack and five ways of carrying them out, and then applies them to the four uses of the protocol.
tldr.outcome: It ends with nine security requirements: mutual authentication, authorisation, replay protection and data-origin authentication are mandatory, while confidentiality and management-object protection are recommended.

today: RFC 5713 is an Informational document published in January 2010, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines no protocol of its own: it sets out a threat model for ANCP and a list of security requirements for the protocol's design, and it points to separate documents for the ANCP framework and for the ANCP MIB module.

sections.title: What ANCP Does and What This Document Adds
sections.content:
The Access Node Control Protocol (ANCP) carries Quality of Service (QoS), service-related and subscriber-related configuration and operations between a Network Access Server (NAS) and an Access Node, such as a Digital Subscriber Line Access Multiplexer (DSLAM). The main goal is to let the NAS configure, manage and control access equipment, and to let the Access Nodes report information back to the NAS.

This document investigates the security threats that all ANCP nodes could encounter. It builds a threat model for ANCP security with the aim of deciding which security functions are required, and then derives security requirements for the protocol. The framework, use cases and general requirements for ANCP come from the ANCP framework document, and the guidelines for protocol security requirements come from RFC 3365.

Three aspects are called out as needing consideration. Message protection, so that signalling content cannot be eavesdropped, modified, injected or replayed while in transit, for both ANCP headers and payloads. Prevention against impersonation, so that an unauthorised device cannot generate an ANCP message and pretend it came from a valid ANCP node. And prevention of denial-of-service attacks, because ANCP nodes and the network have finite resources in state storage, processing power and bandwidth, so the protocol must protect against exhaustion of those resources and must stop ANCP nodes being used to launch attacks on other network elements.

One thing is explicitly out of scope: security policy negotiation, including the authentication and authorisation that define the per-subscriber policy at the policy or AAA server.

sections.title: The System and the Threat Model
sections.content:
The Access Node Control system has six components. The Network Access Server provides access to a service and operates as a client of the AAA protocol, passing authentication information to designated AAA servers and acting on the response. The AAA server authenticates users, authorises access to services and returns authorisation information, including configuration parameters, to be delivered to the user; service usage accounting may also be enabled. The Access Node is a network device, usually in a service provider central office or street cabinet, that terminates access-loop connections from subscribers; for a DSL access loop it is often called a DSLAM. The Customer Premises Equipment sits inside the subscriber's premises, connected at the LAN side of the home gateway. The home gateway connects the customer premises equipment to the Access Node and the access network; for DSL it is a network termination device that may act as a layer 2 bridge or a layer 3 router, in which case it is also called a routing gateway. The aggregation network provides traffic aggregation from multiple Access Nodes towards the NAS, over ATM or Ethernet.

The threat analysis focuses on the ANCP communication between the Access Node and the NAS, though the other components matter for understanding the architecture and what triggers ANCP. The NAS and the Access Node might belong to two different administrative realms, and the threat model and the requirements here assume that case.

In normal operation the NAS receives configuration from the AAA server about a CPE trying to reach the network, and a number of parameters, including QoS information, have to reach the Access Node for them to take effect. ANCP runs between the two to start control requests, and the Access Node answers them and provides information reports. The individual steps are: the Access Node discovers the NAS; it starts protocol communication with the NAS to announce its presence; the two perform a capability exchange; the NAS sends requests; the Access Node processes the requests, authorises the actions and replies, possibly communicating with the home gateway or other nodes to fulfil the commands; and the Access Node provides status reports to the NAS.

Attackers are on-path or off-path. Off-path attackers cannot see the messages exchanged between the Access Node and the NAS; on-path attackers can. Both kinds may be passive, listening to transfers to obtain as much information as possible, or active, taking part in the network operation and able to inject falsified packets. The threat model assumes an off-path adversary at the CPE or the home gateway; an off-path adversary on the internet or a regional network connecting NASes and access networks to network and application service providers; an on-path adversary at network elements between the Access Node and the NAS; an on-path adversary that has taken control over the NAS; and an on-path adversary that has taken control over the Access Node.
sections.plainLanguage: The protocol runs between the provider's central server and the cabinet in the street. The document lists where an attacker could sit, and whether they could only listen or could also send false messages.

sections.title: The Kinds of Attack and the Ways They Are Carried Out
sections.content:
Five kinds of attack are described.

Denial of service. Several denial-of-service attacks can make ANCP nodes malfunction. Where state is established or functions performed without prior authorisation, an adversary can transmit a large number of signalling messages to allocate state at the nodes and consume resources. Denial of service can also stop subscribers reaching services. It can happen at the Access Node or the NAS themselves, where one of them may simply ignore the requests of the other by not replying, which makes the sender retransmit, which may allocate further state at the sender and lead to memory depletion.

Integrity violation. An adversary that gains illegitimate access to the transferred messages can act on them, causing unexpected network behaviour and disturbing network services and the functioning of the network.

Downgrading. Different parts of a network, inside a building, across a public carrier's network or over a private microwave link, may need different levels of protection, and it is often hard to meet conflicting requirements with one mechanism, so a selection of mechanisms and parameters is offered and the protocol has to agree on which to use. An insecure parameter exchange or negotiation protocol lets an adversary force the selection of mechanisms weaker than both parties wanted. Without binding the negotiation to the legitimate parties and protecting it, ANCP would be only as secure as the weakest mechanism offered, such as weak authentication.

Traffic analysis. An adversary placed at the NAS, the Access Node or any other network element can capture all the traversing packets and so gain unauthorised information access, and can gather network information to use later for unauthorised access. It can also help other attacks: capturing the message from the Access Node to the NAS announcing that a DSL line is up reveals information about the connected client, which could be any information about the client, and could show whether the subscriber is at home at that moment.

Management attacks. Because ANCP sessions are configured in the Access Node rather than in the NAS, most ANCP configuration happens on the Access Node, so the management attacks mainly concern the Access Node configuration phase. The AN MIB module could create disclosure and misconfiguration attacks: unauthorised changes to management objects leading to session deletion, a session using an undesired or unsupported protocol, disabling or enabling unwanted ANCP capabilities, ANCP packets going out to the wrong interface and reaching an unintended receiver, harming synchronisation between the Access Node and the NAS, and impacting traffic in the network other than ANCP.

These attacks are carried out in five ways. Message replay, where the adversary eavesdrops, collects signalling messages and replays them later, or at a different place or in a different way, such as cut-and-paste, which can mount denial-of-service and theft-of-service attacks. Faked message injection, injecting false error or response messages to cause unexpected protocol behaviour and a denial-of-service attack, whether at the signalling-protocol level, at the level of specific parameters such as QoS information, or at the transport layer; the discovery protocol in particular is vulnerable to this. Message modification, where the adversary modifies signalling messages, or reorders and delays them, to cause a protocol's process to fail. Man-in-the-middle, where the adversary claims to be a NAS or an Access Node, causing disruption ranging from denial of service to fraud, modifying intercepted messages, dropping or truncating them, or signalling information to an illegitimate entity in place of the right destination so that the protocol appears to keep working while the Access Node contacts the wrong NAS. Eavesdropping, where the collected packets allow traffic analysis or later replay attacks, and may reveal QoS parameters, communication patterns, firewall traversal policy rules, policy information, application identifiers, user identities, NAT bindings, authorisation objects, network configuration and performance information.
sections.plainLanguage: The document lists five things attackers want to do and five ways they go about it, from simply listening to pretending to be the other end of the protocol.

sections.title: The Attacks Applied to the Four ANCP Use Cases
sections.content:
Section 7 applies the attack types to the four ANCP use cases, and also looks at attacks during the protocol-establishment phase, which are mainly on-path denial-of-service and man-in-the-middle attacks. During the session initiation from the Access Node to the NAS, denial of service can affect the session-establishment process, and man-in-the-middle attacks can truncate or modify messages and lead to session-establishment failure. During peering establishment, denial of service can occur during state synchronisation between the Access Node and the NAS, and man-in-the-middle attacks during identity discovery may lead to loss of contact between them. During capabilities negotiation, message replay can cause denial of service, and man-in-the-middle attacks can modify or truncate messages, or downgrade by advertising lesser capabilities.

Dynamic access-loop attributes. This use case carries attributes of the access loop so that the NAS can learn the topology of the access network for QoS scheduling. The rate of the loop may change over time, so advertisement is useful; for a DSL loop this can include the DSL type, the maximum achievable data rate and the maximum rate configured for the loop. On-path active attacks include man-in-the-middle attacks that cause attribute transfer between the Access Node and a forged NAS, producing faked attributes or message modification or truncation; signalling replay causing denial of service; and downgrading by changing the actual data rate of the loop, which affects the downstream shaping from the NAS. Passive on-path attacks are eavesdropping, which reveals attributes and the clients' connection state and so affects their privacy, and traffic analysis, which can allow later unauthorised access to the NAS. Off-path attacks on the internet affect the attribute sharing between the NAS and the AAA or policy server: active ones flood the links to that server or act as a man-in-the-middle to retrieve access-loop configuration for an illegitimate NAS, and passive ones eavesdrop and analyse traffic.

Access-loop configuration. Here the NAS can change access-loop parameters such as the rate dynamically, for example through profiles pre-configured on the Access Nodes, which allows centralised subscriber-related service data. On-path active attacks include denial of service on the Access Node by replaying Configure Request messages; an attacker on the Access Node preventing it from reacting to the NAS request, so the NAS keeps sending the request and keeps allocating state; damaging clients' profiles by adversaries that gained control of the network after learning user information from traffic analysis; and replaying old packets, modifying or injecting faked messages, possibly as a man-in-the-middle, related to a privileged client profile so that the attacker can configure that privileged profile on its own less privileged DSL line, and possibly configure a number of illegitimate lines to hide its identity. Such an adversary can also force configuration parameters other than the selected ones, downgrading the service for a privileged client. Passive on-path attacks learn configuration attributes, which may interest one provider wanting to know what another provider's customers get. Off-path passive attacks on the internet eavesdrop on the configuration retrieval from the AAA or policy server, and off-path active ones can make subscribers' records in that server inaccessible.

Remote connectivity test. The NAS can use ANCP to initiate an access-loop test between the Access Node and the home gateway, so several access-loop technologies can be supported. Most of the attacks here concern network operation. On-path active attacks include a man-in-the-middle during the NAS's trigger to the Access Node, injecting falsified signals or truncating the trigger; message modification during the Subscriber Response that announces the test results, causing the test operation to fail; and an adversary on the Access Node preventing that response, so the NAS keeps triggering the test and allocates more state, which may make the NAS unavailable to the Access Nodes. Off-path active attacks include causing denial of service during the test, in the case of an ATM-based access loop when the Access Node generates loopback cells, by replaying signals; and truncating messages during the test, which can lead to service disruption because the test is assumed to have failed.

Multicast. ANCP could be used to exchange information that lets the Access Node replicate inline with the subscriber's policy and configuration, and lets the NAS follow subscribers' multicast membership and control the replication the Access Node performs. Four multicast use cases are expected: multicast conditional access, multicast admission control, multicast accounting and spontaneous admission response. The attacks are mostly active. On-path active attacks include denial of service, by message replay, leaving some subscribers unable to reach a stream or able to reach it only at reduced bandwidth, which affects the quality of a possible video stream, and by tampering with white or black list configuration or with the bandwidth-admission-control mechanism; an adversary on the NAS preventing it from reacting to the Access Node's requests for lists or admission control, so the Access Node keeps sending requests and allocating state, with the same happening in reverse for admission control, which may make the NAS unavailable to the Access Nodes; and man-in-the-middle attacks between the Access Node and a forged NAS or a forged Access Node and the NAS, leading to message modification that can downgrade the service for legitimate subscribers, message truncation that breaks the continuity of service, message replay leading to denial of service or service fraud, and message modification to tamper with accounting information, to avoid service charges or to increase them for other users. Off-path active attacks include denial of service through replay of join or leave requests by the home gateway or CPE, which frequently triggers ANCP activity, and through generating many IGMP joins and leaves, leading to a very high rate of ANCP queries and responses.
sections.plainLanguage: The document then goes through the four things ANCP is used for, and for each one lists what an attacker could do to it.

sections.title: The Security Requirements
sections.content:
The requirements are derived from the attack types above, and they say what the protocol solution must offer.

  • It MUST offer authentication of the Access Node to the NAS.
  • It MUST offer authentication of the NAS to the Access Node.
  • It MUST allow authorisation to take place at the NAS and at the Access Node.
  • It MUST offer replay protection.
  • It MUST provide data-origin authentication.
  • It MUST be robust against denial-of-service attacks, and in this context it MUST consider a specific mechanism for the denial of service a user might create by sending many IGMP messages.
  • It SHOULD offer confidentiality protection.
  • It SHOULD ensure that operations in the default configuration guarantee a low number of Access Node and NAS protocol interactions.
  • It SHOULD ensure the access control of the management objects, and possibly encrypt the values of those objects when sending them over the networks.

The last two SHOULD requirements are worth noting for what they say about everyday behaviour. A default installation should not be chatty, and the management objects that hold the configuration should be access-controlled, with their values possibly encrypted in transit.
sections.plainLanguage: Both ends must prove who they are, messages must not be replayed or forged, and the protocol must survive a flood of traffic without falling over.

sections.title: Scope and the Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document's own security considerations section says it focuses on security threats, deriving a threat model for ANCP and presenting the security requirements to be considered for the design of ANCP.

Two boundaries are worth stating. Security policy negotiation, including the authentication and authorisation used to define the per-subscriber policy at the policy or AAA server, is out of scope. And although ANCP is not itself involved in the communication between the NAS and the AAA or policy server, the security of that communication matters for ANCP security, so the threat model and the requirements here take into account the data transfer between the NAS and the AAA server when that data is used within the ANCP operation.
sections.plainLanguage: What the protocol does not cover is deciding the subscriber's policy, which happens on the AAA server instead. But the link to that server still matters, because ANCP carries the results of it.

THE FIVE KINDS OF ATTACK DESCRIBED IN RFC 5713

items.title: Denial of service
items.text: Flooding the protocol so that state and memory run out, or one end simply stops replying.

items.title: Integrity violation
items.text: Changing a message in transit so that the network behaves in an unexpected way.

items.title: Downgrading
items.text: Forcing the negotiation to pick weaker protection than both sides wanted.

items.title: Traffic analysis
items.text: Learning from the messages that pass, including whether a subscriber is at home.

items.title: Management attacks
items.text: Changing the configuration objects on the Access Node, for example deleting a session.
